items.title: The Attention Brief #04 — What AI use tells us about learning
items.summary: This week’s clearest distinction is between wanting to use AI, feeling that learning is going well, and experiencing the costs of that use. Those outcomes call for different evidence and different questions about attention.
items.content_html:
Week of Monday, November 9, 2026

What AI use tells us about learning

Sources originally published 2026-11-02 through 2026-11-08 (UTC). Older background sources are not included.

This week’s clearest distinction is between wanting to use AI, feeling that learning is going well, and experiencing the costs of that use. Those outcomes call for different evidence and different questions about attention.

An appealing AI tool can fit into a learner’s routine without telling us whether it improves independent learning. This week’s selected readings make that distinction useful: one examines willingness to use AI, another connects reported dependency with persistence and perceived learning, and a third explores adult learners’ wellbeing. Read together, they suggest an evaluation agenda, rather than a shared verdict on AI. Ask what people are willing to try, what effort they retain, and what the experience costs them. Then measure those outcomes separately.

Ease and confidence are questions about uptake

Isaac Davor and colleagues surveyed university students in Ghana about their intention to use generative AI. Students who expected the tools to be useful and easy to use reported greater willingness to use them; anxiety about digital learning was associated with lower willingness. These were responses collected at one point in time.

The implication is a distinction to preserve when evaluating a tool: an inviting interface and a reassuring experience concern uptake. They do not, by themselves, demonstrate better learning. This survey identifies associations with intention, not the effects of an intervention on knowledge, performance, or sustained attention.

Digital learning anxiety and UTAUT predictors of university students’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence in Ghana

Look beyond how often a tool is used

ShuFei Li and colleagues examined students’ reported AI dependency, ability to sustain effort, and perceptions of their learning. Greater dependency was associated with less persistence and a small negative overall association with perceived learning. The remaining direct association, after accounting for effort regulation, was not statistically distinguishable from zero. Those are different estimates, not contradictory conclusions.

This was a cross-sectional survey, so the pattern cannot establish what caused what. The outcomes were learners’ assessments, not demonstrated achievement. Unaccounted classroom clustering also limits confidence in the small overall association. For evaluation, the useful question is whether learners keep working through difficulty, rather than treating frequency of AI use as a sufficient measure of dependence.

Generative AI dependency and perceived learning outcomes among university students: an indirect association involving effort regulation

A positive average can conceal individual strain

Michael Agyemang Adarkwah and colleagues combined a survey with accounts from adult learners at a Ghanaian university. The survey’s overall picture of digital wellbeing was positive, but some respondents reported disturbed sleep, physical discomfort, changes in eating, or less exercise. The high score on the reverse-coded physical scale reflected relatively little reported strain; it was not evidence of improved physical health.

These are participants’ reports of their experience, not proof that AI caused changes in health. Alongside the other readings, the study points to another evaluation question: whose experience disappears inside an average? Asking about persistence or willingness to use a tool should leave room to ask about discomfort and disruption as well.

Storying digital well-being and quality of life in Ghanaian adult learners’ use of generative AI

What happens when a learner accepts less assistance?

Could a small pause before accepting an AI answer preserve effort without making a task unnecessarily frustrating? The intention survey by Isaac Davor and colleagues, the dependency analysis by ShuFei Li and colleagues, and the wellbeing account by Michael Agyemang Adarkwah and colleagues suggest different outcomes to track in such a test. Measure willingness to continue, the reasoning a learner can explain independently, and reported strain separately. This is a proposed comparison; these papers do not establish that the pause would work.

Storying digital well-being and quality of life in Ghanaian adult learners’ use of generative AI · Digital learning anxiety and UTAUT predictors of university students’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence in Ghana · Generative AI dependency and perceived learning outcomes among university students: an indirect association involving effort regulation

Make one judgment visible

Before accepting an AI answer, write down one decision you still need to make yourself. Afterward, record the evidence for that decision and anything that remains uncertain.

An untested reflection prompt inspired by the questions above, not a proven attention intervention.

Can a learner explain the reasoning without the tool, and what effort or discomfort accompanied getting there?

items.title: The Attention Brief #03 — When AI helps, what do we still do ourselves?
items.summary: Checking an AI answer, solving a problem without it, and choosing what it can access are different kinds of control. This week’s readings make those differences concrete, from students asking for math help to phone owners protecting their messages.
items.content_html:
Week of Monday, November 2, 2026

When AI helps, what do we still do ourselves?

Sources originally published 2026-10-26 through 2026-11-01 (UTC). Older background sources are not included.

Checking an AI answer, solving a problem without it, and choosing what it can access are different kinds of control. This week’s readings make those differences concrete, from students asking for math help to phone owners protecting their messages.

It is easy to call someone an active AI user. It is harder to say what they are actually doing: checking a claim, working through a problem, or simply keeping a conversation going. This week, start with those actions. Two studies compare students’ accounts or chat behavior with different outcomes. A prototype study asks what makes a chatbot feel like a classmate. Two EFF essays tackle a separate, practical problem: how people can limit or challenge an automated system. The useful connections are specific, not a single verdict on whether AI helps us think.

Saying you checked an answer is different from solving the next problem

In Akgun and Toker’s survey of 891 college students in the US and Türkiye, students who reported coordinating work with AI and reworking its suggestions were also more likely to report thinking critically about its output. Their critical-thinking measure was a yes/no answer, followed by a checklist of tactics such as checking AI output against other sources. Nobody took a critical-thinking test. The survey connects students’ accounts of related habits; it does not show that AI improved their ability.

Abdelghani, Kaiser and Murayama took a different approach: they observed 112 ninth-graders in three German schools practicing math with Mistral, a general-purpose chatbot, then tested them without AI. Their analysis of 89 students linked a shift toward requests for explanations or methods with better immediate test scores, after accounting for initial scores and other chat measures. On average, though, requests shifted in the opposite direction. The promising clue is how a conversation changes, rather than a count of “good” prompts. The paper’s text and table report different p-values for the same model comparison. The discrepancy does not reverse the authors’ conclusion, but it needs clarification. And observation alone cannot show that changing someone’s prompts would improve their learning.

When Does GenAI Use Support Critical Thinking? A Cross-Cultural Structural Account of Transactive Memory with GenAI · arXiv preprint v1 · Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI · arXiv preprint v1

A chatbot can feel friendly while getting the math wrong

In Lin and colleagues’ Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning, seven researchers spent about 20 minutes imagining themselves as students solving equations with a chatbot. In interviews, they described feeling less judged than with a human classmate. But collaboration broke down when the bot rushed to an answer, took over the pace, or agreed too readily. Mistakes made it feel more like a peer to some participants and less useful to others.

One illustrated exchange makes the problem tangible: for x² + 5x − 6 = 0, the bot asks for numbers that multiply to +6, when they should multiply to −6. This is an error in a depicted example, not a measured error rate. The interviews tell us what these adults liked or resisted; they do not tell us whether students learned. Set beside Abdelghani and colleagues’ math study, the design question becomes sharper: can a chatbot leave room for a learner’s ideas, help them notice errors, and still prepare them to solve a problem alone? That is a question to test, not a benefit either study has established.

Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI · arXiv preprint v1 · Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning · arXiv preprint v1

Control also means being able to say no, or ask for another look

EFF’s guide to excluding apps from Siri AI gives a concrete example of setting a boundary before a system acts. EFF reports that excluding Messages removes Siri’s ability to read and reply to messages. The loss of convenience is part of the trade-off: a meaningful restriction should stop the assistant doing something. This is EFF’s account of the settings, not our own software or security test.

EFF’s essay on election moderation tackles what happens after a system acts. When a platform removes a post, the writer needs a way to explain context an automated filter may have missed. EFF argues for appeals to human reviewers, clearer disclosure and oversight. These are policy proposals, not measured proof that the safeguards work. Unlike the learning studies, these essays are about permission and recourse: who can prevent an action, and who can challenge it afterwards. A tool that helps someone think and a tool they can refuse need different kinds of evaluation.

Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI · Publisher article · Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better · Publisher article

What should we ask a learning tool to leave behind?

A useful next test would connect the experience of using a chatbot with what a learner can do later. Lin and colleagues’ interviews suggest choices worth comparing, such as letting the learner set the pace rather than jumping ahead. Abdelghani and colleagues’ study points to a way of checking the result: look at the conversation, then assess the learner without AI. A follow-up could compare specific designs and repeat the assessment after a delay. That would help distinguish a pleasant interaction, immediate success and learning that lasts. It would still be a learning test, not an answer to EFF’s separate questions about privacy or appeal rights.

Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI · arXiv preprint v1 · Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning · arXiv preprint v1 · Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI · Publisher article · Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better · Publisher article

Try explaining it without the chat

After asking AI for help with a problem, close the conversation and explain the next step in your own words. Note where you get stuck.

A personal reflection prompt, not a proven way to improve learning.

After the chat ends, what can the learner explain or solve on their own?

A few useful terms

preprints
Research manuscripts shared publicly, usually before formal review by other researchers is complete. The review status of these three papers is unverified.
p-values
A low p-value means results at least this extreme would be unusual if there were no relationship and the statistical model’s assumptions held. It does not measure importance or prove cause and effect.
recourse
A way to challenge a decision and seek a correction, such as asking a human to review a removed post.

Sources & reading details

The three research papers are preprints; peer review is unverified. They do not establish that AI causes better learning. This edition was rewritten against the linked source versions and reviewed in a separate AI pass, not by a human expert or through replication. The EFF articles are attributed commentary checked in current HTML; their original-week wording, software behavior and linked claims were not independently verified. Source coverage is partial. Details and source versions are listed below.

signals.title: Saying you checked an answer is different from solving the next problem
signals.text:
In Akgun and Toker’s survey of 891 college students in the US and Türkiye, students who reported coordinating work with AI and reworking its suggestions were also more likely to report thinking critically about its output. Their critical-thinking measure was a yes/no answer, followed by a checklist of tactics such as checking AI output against other sources. Nobody took a critical-thinking test. The survey connects students’ accounts of related habits; it does not show that AI improved their ability.

Abdelghani, Kaiser and Murayama took a different approach: they observed 112 ninth-graders in three German schools practicing math with Mistral, a general-purpose chatbot, then tested them without AI. Their analysis of 89 students linked a shift toward requests for explanations or methods with better immediate test scores, after accounting for initial scores and other chat measures. On average, though, requests shifted in the opposite direction. The promising clue is how a conversation changes, rather than a count of “good” prompts. The paper’s text and table report different p-values for the same model comparison. The discrepancy does not reverse the authors’ conclusion, but it needs clarification. And observation alone cannot show that changing someone’s prompts would improve their learning.

signals.title: A chatbot can feel friendly while getting the math wrong
signals.text:
In Lin and colleagues’ Exploring AI Peer in Collaborative Mathematics Learning, seven researchers spent about 20 minutes imagining themselves as students solving equations with a chatbot. In interviews, they described feeling less judged than with a human classmate. But collaboration broke down when the bot rushed to an answer, took over the pace, or agreed too readily. Mistakes made it feel more like a peer to some participants and less useful to others.

One illustrated exchange makes the problem tangible: for x² + 5x − 6 = 0, the bot asks for numbers that multiply to +6, when they should multiply to −6. This is an error in a depicted example, not a measured error rate. The interviews tell us what these adults liked or resisted; they do not tell us whether students learned. Set beside Abdelghani and colleagues’ math study, the design question becomes sharper: can a chatbot leave room for a learner’s ideas, help them notice errors, and still prepare them to solve a problem alone? That is a question to test, not a benefit either study has established.

signals.title: Control also means being able to say no, or ask for another look
signals.text:
EFF’s guide to excluding apps from Siri AI gives a concrete example of setting a boundary before a system acts. EFF reports that excluding Messages removes Siri’s ability to read and reply to messages. The loss of convenience is part of the trade-off: a meaningful restriction should stop the assistant doing something. This is EFF’s account of the settings, not our own software or security test.

EFF’s essay on election moderation tackles what happens after a system acts. When a platform removes a post, the writer needs a way to explain context an automated filter may have missed. EFF argues for appeals to human reviewers, clearer disclosure and oversight. These are policy proposals, not measured proof that the safeguards work. Unlike the learning studies, these essays are about permission and recourse: who can prevent an action, and who can challenge it afterwards. A tool that helps someone think and a tool they can refuse need different kinds of evaluation.

tension.title: What should we ask a learning tool to leave behind?
tension.text: A useful next test would connect the experience of using a chatbot with what a learner can do later. Lin and colleagues’ interviews suggest choices worth comparing, such as letting the learner set the pace rather than jumping ahead. Abdelghani and colleagues’ study points to a way of checking the result: look at the conversation, then assess the learner without AI. A follow-up could compare specific designs and repeat the assessment after a delay. That would help distinguish a pleasant interaction, immediate success and learning that lasts. It would still be a learning test, not an answer to EFF’s separate questions about privacy or appeal rights.

items.title: The Attention Brief #02 — Which thinking stays with the learner?
items.summary: This collection separates an enjoyable AI interaction, a stronger assisted product, and what someone can do independently. Research and commentary offer different ways to examine that distinction; they do not establish a shared causal effect on attention.
items.content_html:
Week of Monday, October 26, 2026

Which thinking stays with the learner?

Historical collection, including earlier sources; not a strict previous-week digest.

This collection separates an enjoyable AI interaction, a stronger assisted product, and what someone can do independently. Research and commentary offer different ways to examine that distinction; they do not establish a shared causal effect on attention.

The useful question in this collection is what an intervention changes, and how we would know. A pleasant learning experience, a polished assignment, and independent understanding require different evidence. The studies below measure parts of that picture in particular educational settings. The essays ask broader questions about media design and control. Read together, they suggest questions for future comparisons rather than a verdict on whether AI helps or harms thinking. This is the October collection week, including older material newly indexed by the Observatory; it is not a claim that every source was published this week.

A better learning experience needs its own outcome test

A randomized classroom trial of self-regulation chatbots found better enjoyment and less boredom than general-purpose ChatGPT. The emotionally supportive version also improved some regulation indicators in interaction traces. Knowledge and transfer gains, however, did not differ significantly between conditions, including at follow-up. The short session, follow-up attrition and weak reliability of some tests limit conclusions. A separate reflective-dashboard study reports improvements in learning behaviors and academic performance during a longer quasi-experimental intervention. Our access to that second study is abstract-based, so its reported gains cannot settle questions about allocation, measurement or lasting transfer. These results concern different interventions and outcomes; neither comparison establishes a general improvement in sustained attention.

Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes · Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education

The assisted product can hide the learning question

In a university writing study, open AI collaboration produced the strongest observed work while assistance was available. Bounded support combined with reflection showed the most favorable profile on the later independent assessment. The design used intact classes, so class and condition were partly confounded; the support package also combined several ingredients. Its assessment measured near transfer within the same course and genre. Kucirkova’s commentary on children’s media asks a related design question: does an engaging experience leave room to process it? That essay supplies an argument about pacing, not an experimental test of AI or a finding that slower media always teaches better. The connection is a question about participation, not evidence of one common mechanism.

Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes · Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV

Control involves choices made along the way

Wintermeier’s commentary argues that the image of a single AI kill switch obscures distributed systems and the human decisions surrounding them. It is a governance argument, not a trial of technical safeguards. At a different scale, the writing study makes it useful to ask which decisions students retain during assisted work. Its results do not establish that any one delegation rule caused independent learning gains. The connection between these sources is interpretive: examining control requires attention to ongoing decisions, not only the finished output or a final intervention. A governance essay and a classroom comparison cannot validate each other’s claims, but they can help make that research question more precise.

Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI · Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes

When and how to rely on AI

The staged-use essay proposes introducing substantive AI assistance after learners demonstrate readiness. Our reading is abstract-based: this is an instructional proposal, not a test showing that a particular sequence improves learning.

The higher-education study examines course work and students’ accounts of AI use. Its authors interpret the pattern as gradual normalization alongside continuing concerns about authentic learning. The study used naturally occurring data without experimental control, so this does not show that normalization caused better outcomes.

The theory-building review organizes evidence around learners monitoring their work, deciding when to trust AI, and sharing responsibility for regulation. Its varied studies and single-author synthesis limit common conclusions. Separately, the technostress survey links greater reported AI-related strain with lower engagement and adaptability. Its cross-sectional, self-report design cannot establish cause and effect.

These readings sharpen three questions to test: when assistance becomes available, how learners evaluate it, and how demanding it feels.

From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education · Self-regulated approaches to students’ generative AI use in higher education · The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review · Generative AI technostress and learning engagement among Chinese university students: a moderated mediation model of academic adaptability and AI literacy

How much help preserves useful practice?

The unresolved design problem is how to support people while leaving meaningful opportunities to judge, explain and revise. Greater enjoyment may matter without producing a measurable learning advantage. Stronger work with assistance may also differ from independent performance. Future studies could vary the kind of support, observe what learners actually do, and assess comparable tasks after assistance is removed. Longer follow-up and wider transfer tests would help distinguish a short-lived classroom pattern from a durable change. Sustained attention needs its own direct measurement; engagement ratings, writing scores and time on task cannot answer that question by themselves.

Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes · Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes · Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education

Keep one decision visible

Before using AI on a task, write down one judgment you want to make yourself. Afterwards, note what evidence changed that judgment.

A reflection prompt, not a tested intervention.

What evidence would show that a tool improves the learner’s own judgment after the assistance ends?

The reflective-dashboard account is abstract-based; the media and governance pieces are commentary. This is a research digest, not an independently reviewed systematic review.

items.title: The Attention Brief #01 — Who's doing the thinking?
items.summary: Across the opening collection’s education studies, public essays, and adjacent attention research, a recurring question is who retains judgment when technology makes work easier. The material raises promising ideas but doesn't establish a single causal answer.
items.content_html:
Week of Monday, October 19, 2026

The question isn't how much AI we use. It's which thinking we keep.

Historical collection, including earlier sources; not a strict previous-week digest.

Across the opening collection’s education studies, public essays, and adjacent attention research, a recurring question is who retains judgment when technology makes work easier. The material raises promising ideas but doesn't establish a single causal answer.

Hello from the Observatory. There's a tempting way to frame AI and attention: more AI means less thinking. This opening reading set makes that story look too simple. Some authors describe AI as a scaffold for problem-solving; others worry that efficient delegation becomes habitual substitution. Meanwhile, the broader attention literature reminds us that distraction has many sources besides AI. The more useful question may be: what does a tool help us do ourselves, and what does it quietly do in our place?

The quality of AI use matters more than the usage count

One EFL study reports an association between AI literacy, AI-assisted problem-solving, and critical thinking; other education sources describe efficiency-first use or warn about unsupervised offloading. These findings and arguments point toward examining how people engage with AI, without proving which design improves learning.

Beyond AI Use: How AI Literacy Is Linked to Critical Thinking through AI-Assisted Problem-Solving Ability and AI Reliance · AI-Assisted Translation Pedagogy for Critical Thinking: A Pathway to Sustainable Education · Artificial Intelligence Usage, Cognitive Offloading, and Academic Performance among Rural Undergraduate Students: A Sequential Mediation Model

Distraction sits inside a larger social and cognitive setting

The adolescent attention study links academic impact with stress and social-media duration. Research on task switching in insomnia examines a different mechanism, while reporting on children's TV points to commercial design incentives. These are useful adjacent lenses, not direct evidence that generative AI causes attention fragmentation.

Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis · Disrupted network reconfiguration during task switching in insomnia: the role of sleep-related attentional bias · Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV - The Guardian

An intervention can help—or become another form of control

The opening collection includes speculative work on wearable urge regulation, critiques of AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring, and an empirical study of selective parental alerts. Their targets differ, but together they suggest a design question: how can a tool support attention without claiming to measure or control someone's inner state?

AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation · AI-MEDIATED WELLBEING SURVEILLANCE AND THE BOUNDARY OF PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY · Parental Notification Gaps in ChatGPT-5: An Empirical Study

When does helpful scaffolding become outsourcing?

Some sources frame AI assistance as a route to better problem-solving. Others argue that repeated delegation can reduce opportunities to practice judgment. These claims are not experimentally settled across settings; they're competing possibilities that future designs can test.

The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Cognitive Scaffolding, Substitution, and the Risk of Deskilling · Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning

The 45-second ‘thinking first’ test

Before your next AI request, write one sentence saying what you think the answer is. Then ask for a counterargument or a hint rather than the completed answer. Notice whether your own reasoning changes.

A personal reflection prompt, not a proven intervention.

One question to keep: If an AI tool makes the task faster, what evidence would show that it also made our thinking better?

_observatory.note: New source records have been indexed. A cross-source editorial synthesis has not yet been reviewed and published.
_observatory.subject: The Attention Edit #01 — Who's doing the thinking?
_observatory.headline: The question isn't how much AI we use. It's which thinking we keep.
_observatory.deck: Across the opening collection’s education studies, public essays, and adjacent attention research, a recurring question is who retains judgment when technology makes work easier. The material raises promising ideas but doesn't establish a single causal answer.
_observatory.letter: Hello from the Observatory. There's a tempting way to frame AI and attention: more AI means less thinking. This opening reading set makes that story look too simple. Some authors describe AI as a scaffold for problem-solving; others worry that efficient delegation becomes habitual substitution. Meanwhile, the broader attention literature reminds us that distraction has many sources besides AI. The more useful question may be: what does a tool help us do ourselves, and what does it quietly do in our place?

experiment.title: The 45-second ‘thinking first’ test
experiment.text: Before your next AI request, write one sentence saying what you think the answer is. Then ask for a counterargument or a hint rather than the completed answer. Notice whether your own reasoning changes.
experiment.caution: A personal reflection prompt, not a proven intervention.

_observatory.closer: One question to keep: If an AI tool makes the task faster, what evidence would show that it also made our thinking better?
_observatory.editorial_note: Editorial synthesis prepared from all source-backed items in the opening reading collection. Some readings rely on abstracts or publisher synopses; cross-source patterns are interpretations, not causal conclusions.

signals.short: It's about delegation, not just adoption
signals.title: The quality of AI use matters more than the usage count
signals.text: One EFL study reports an association between AI literacy, AI-assisted problem-solving, and critical thinking; other education sources describe efficiency-first use or warn about unsupervised offloading. These findings and arguments point toward examining how people engage with AI, without proving which design improves learning.
sources: Beyond AI Use: How AI Literacy Is Linked

signals.title: Distraction sits inside a larger social and cognitive setting
signals.text: The adolescent attention study links academic impact with stress and social-media duration. Research on task switching in insomnia examines a different mechanism, while reporting on children's TV points to commercial design incentives. These are useful adjacent lenses, not direct evidence that generative AI causes attention fragmentation.

signals.short: Focus tools raise questions about agency
signals.title: An intervention can help—or become another form of control
signals.text: The opening collection includes speculative work on wearable urge regulation, critiques of AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring, and an empirical study of selective parental alerts. Their targets differ, but together they suggest a design question: how can a tool support attention without claiming to measure or control someone's inner state?

tension.label: THE PRODUCTIVE TENSION
tension.title: When does helpful scaffolding become outsourcing?
tension.text: Some sources frame AI assistance as a route to better problem-solving. Others argue that repeated delegation can reduce opportunities to practice judgment. These claims are not experimentally settled across settings; they're competing possibilities that future designs can test.
